title: Jude and the Verdict
premise: Marguerite Eriksen, a true-crime podcaster who has never abandoned a case, reopens the 1979 disappearance of Jude Calloway — the coldest missing-person file on record. When she finds Jude's diary in an estate sale and discovers entries written after the disappearance date, she realizes Jude survived, hid in plain sight, and left behind a coded ledger naming everyone complicit in her vanishing: a judge, a sheriff, and the town's founding family. As Marguerite decodes the ledger, someone begins silencing the descendants of those named, and she must choose between broadcasting the truth that will make her career and protecting the fragile found family of survivors Jude assembled over forty years. In the end, Marguerite closes the case not by exposing Jude's location but by letting the verdict be delivered on Jude's terms — justice outside the law, at the cost of the story of a lifetime.
about_author: Felix Lockridge is the pen name of a former court stenographer who spent two decades transcribing trials before turning to fiction. They write mysteries about people the legal system failed, from a farmhouse full of rescued typewriters.

chapters.title: The Coldest File
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. She closes her ninth solved case with a triumphant episode finale, then receives an anonymous package: Jude Calloway's diary from 1979, last entry dated three weeks after her disappearance. The emotional beat is restless triumph curdling into obsession — a case that shouldn't exist.

chapters.title: Estate Sale Ghosts
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. She traces the diary to the estate of a deceased archivist in Hollow Creek and interviews the archivist's wary niece, Delia. Someone else asked about the diary a week ago. Beat: first chill of competition — or threat.

chapters.title: Entries After the End
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, interleaved with diary excerpts. The post-disappearance entries are coded, referencing 'the ledger' and 'the ones who signed.' Marguerite realizes Jude lived for years after vanishing. Beat: vertigo — the victim was an author all along.

chapters.title: Hollow Creek Welcomes You
chapters.summary: Marguerite arrives in Hollow Creek under a false pretext, renting a room above a diner run by Sam Okafor, a warm ex-nurse who collects strays. Sheriff Brandt, grandson of the 1979 sheriff, politely warns her off. Beat: a town smiling with its teeth closed.

chapters.title: The Found Family
chapters.summary: Sam's POV. We learn the diner's back booth hosts a quiet circle: Delia, retired teacher Ruth, mechanic Theo — all connected to 1979, all bound by something unspoken. Sam recognizes what Marguerite is digging for. Beat: tenderness guarding a wound.

chapters.title: Judge Ashford's Signature
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Decoding the diary's cipher (a judge's gavel doodle as key), she matches names to Hollow Creek's founding families. First name decoded: Judge Ashford, who signed Jude's commitment order days before she vanished. Beat: the case snaps open like a lock.

chapters.title: What Ruth Remembers
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV, 1979 flashback. A teenage Ruth saw Jude the night she disappeared — alive, running toward the quarry, chased by two men. She never told anyone. Present-day Ruth burns a letter when Marguerite gets close. Beat: guilt as a lifelong tenant.

chapters.title: A Warning in the Mailbox
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Her rental is searched; the diary's hiding place disturbed but untouched. A note appears: SOME CASES STAY CLOSED. Sheriff Brandt offers 'protection' that feels like surveillance. Beat: fear sharpening into defiance.

chapters.title: The Ledger Hidden in Plain Sight
chapters.summary: Marguerite and Delia discover the ledger isn't a book — it's the memorial quilt hanging in the diner, stitched by Jude herself, each panel a coded account. Sam goes pale: he's slept beneath it for thirty years. Beat: awe and betrayal braided together.

chapters.title: Descendants
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. One by one, the living descendants of the named families receive copies of their ancestors' pages. Theo's garage burns that night. Beat: the past collecting its debts, and the town fracturing along old seams.

chapters.title: Brandt's Confession
chapters.summary: Sheriff Brandt's POV. He found his grandfather's journal years ago and buried it to protect the family name — and because he was a boy who loved the legend of Jude more than the truth. Now he gives Marguerite the journal. Beat: complicity inherited, honesty chosen late.

chapters.title: Jude Was Here
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Following the journal and quilt codes to the quarry, she finds a sealed root cellar: Jude lived there until 1994, walls papered with evidence, photographs, and letters to a child — Delia. Beat: grief and wonder; the missing woman never stopped testifying.

chapters.title: Delia's Mother
chapters.summary: Delia's POV. Her mother was Jude's daughter, given away the night of the disappearance; the archivist was raising the ledger for Delia's inheritance. Delia rages at Marguerite for dragging it into the light. Beat: found family cracking under the weight of blood secrets.

chapters.title: The Man Who Signed Twice
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. The final decoded name isn't from 1979 — it's current: the estate-sale buyer who asked about the diary is Ashford's grandson, a sitting magistrate destroying the ledger page by page. Beat: the cold case turns hot and present-tense.

chapters.title: Vanishing Pattern
chapters.summary: Sam's POV. Ruth disappears; her cottage staged to look like she fled. Sam recognizes the staging — he once nursed a man who described doing exactly this in '79. Beat: history repeating with terrible fluency.

chapters.title: Broadcast
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Against every instinct, she airs a partial episode: the quilt, the cellar, Ruth's face. It forces the magistrate's hand but paints a target on the diner family. Beat: the price of survival made explicit — truth as both shield and flare.

chapters.title: The Quarry at Night
chapters.summary: Climax part one, Marguerite's POV. Lured by a message claiming Ruth is alive, Marguerite walks into the quarry cellar. The magistrate arrives to burn the last evidence — with her inside it. Beat: terror, and the cold clarity of someone who refuses to die mid-sentence.

chapters.title: Verdict
chapters.summary: Climax part two, rotating POVs. Sam, Delia, Theo, and Brandt arrive — the found family executing Jude's own contingency plan hidden in the quilt's final panel. The magistrate is trapped, recorded, and delivered to state police alongside forty years of Jude's testimony. Beat: justice rendered by the people the law forgot.

chapters.title: Ruth, Returned
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. Rescued from the magistrate's boat house, Ruth finally tells the whole night of 1979 aloud. Her testimony completes the record. Beat: release — fifty years of held breath let out in one long exhale.

chapters.title: Where the Diary Ends
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. The recovered evidence reveals Jude's last entry: she chose to disappear again in 1994 to protect Delia, leaving the ledger as her verdict. A fresh envelope arrives — new handwriting, dated last month. Beat: hope arriving disguised as an ending.

chapters.title: The Case She Won't Close
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Offered a network deal to expose everything including Jude's survival, Marguerite instead airs a final episode closing the case officially — and privately mails her research to a P.O. box in the next county. Beat: the cost paid gladly; some truths belong to the people who earned them.

chapters.title: Jude and the Verdict
chapters.summary: Jude's POV, brief and final. An elderly woman in a coastal town reads Marguerite's letter, listens to the last episode, and adds one line to a worn diary: 'Case closed. Family found.' She sets a place at her table for a visitor she already knows is coming. Beat: peace — the verdict was always belonging.
